newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu fighting surprise Jerusalem housing plan.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu fighting surprise Jerusalem housing plan.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is fighting a plan to build tens of homes for Jews in the heart of an Arab East Jerusalem neighbourhood, Netanyahu's office said.

"The prime minister heard late at night from the mayor of Jerusalem on the decision taken on the issue...the prime minister is working to prevent implementation of the plan," Netanyahu's office said in a hastily prepared statement on Thursday.

Israel Television reported late on Thursday that the Jerusalem municipality had granted a permit to Irving Moskowitz, a U.S. Jewish businessman who bankrolls Jewish settlement in occupied areas, to build tens of Jewish homes in the Ras al-Amoud neighbourhood.
"He is permitted to build tomorrow and it is impossible to halt it," the television reported. Palestinians have called the plan a "time bomb".

The move comes with Israeli-Palestine Liberation Organisation peace talks deep in crisis and Middle East tensions high over Israel's groundbreaking last March for a Jewish settlement on an Arab East Jerusalem hill.

Israel's Jerusalem municipal planning commission gave conditional approval last December to a plan to build 132 homes for Jews in the heart of the neighbourhood of 11,000 Palestinians, sparking Arab warnings that a final go ahead would spark violence.
The plan required the approval of Interior Minister Eli Suissa but was later shelved.
The television reported a city committee had approved a scaled back version of the plan, limited to tens of homes, which apparently did not need ministerial approval.
"The prime minister said tonight that he opposes the decision taken today in the municipality to start building now in Ras al-Amoud," Netanyahu's office said.
Miami-based Moskowitz says he owns the 3.5 acre (1.3 hectare) plot in Ras al-Amoud neighbourhood. The claim is disputed by Palestinian officials.

Palestinians have warned the plan could spark rage on the scale of bloody Israeli-PLO gunbattles that erupted last September when Netanyahu opened an entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem's Old City. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
The television said it was not clear how a Jerusalem municipal committee could approve so sensitive a plan.
"The Jerusalem municipality decided suddenly, now, that it can not oppose it. Perhaps from a legal perspective justice is with him (Moskowitz)," the television reported.

The status of East Jerusalem is one of the most volatile issues dividing Israelis and Palestinians. The PLO wants East Jerusalem as capital of a future Palestinian state. Israel says both sides of the city form its "united and eternal" capital.
Palestinians say Israeli moves in East Jerusalem are aimed at preempting peace talks on the city's fate. There are now some 160,000 Jews in East Jerusalem and 155,000 Palestinians.
